                                         3D scene-language understanding aims to jointly interpret
                                                                                                            Recently, Chat-Scene [13] introduced an Object-Centric
                                         3D environments and natural language, serving as a funda-
                                                                                                         3D LLM framework that decomposes an input 3D scene into
                                         mental basis for multi-modal reasoning in applications such
                                                                                                         a set of object proposals using a pretrained detector [21].
                                         as robotic navigation and embodied agents. Traditionally,
                                                                                                         Each object is represented by an identifier token and its
                                         3D scene-language tasks have relied on specialized, task-
                                                                                                         instance-level 3D and 2D features, enabling object-centric
                                         specific models (e.g., grounding, captioning, and question-
                                                                                                         reasoning via LLMs [10, 36]. Following this paradigm,

Figure 2. Overview of 3D Scene-Language Understanding and an Object-Centric Framework. (a) Examples of 3D reasoning tasks,
including visual grounding and dense captioning. Object identifiers (e.g., <OBJ000>) are utilized to reference and ground target objects
during the conversation. (b) The object-centric 3D LLM consists of an input construction module and an LLM decoder. Unlike prior works
focusing on input construction, we emphasize the decoder to enhance 3D reasoning.

 (a) Point Cloud and Instruction                                                                                                                                               (b) Geometry-adaptive Mask                                                                                                                                                                    (c) Instruction-aware Mask

Figure 3. Overview of 3D Spatial Language Instruction Mask (3D-SLIM). (a) Illustration of the input 3D point cloud and user instruction,
which are subsequently encoded as object and instruction tokens. For simplicity, only a small subset of object and instruction tokens is
depicted. (b) The Geometry-adaptive Mask dynamically modulates object-object attention based on spatial proximity and local density;
objects in denser regions attend to an expanded set of neighbors, whereas those in sparse areas focus on fewer neighbors. (c) The Instruction-
aware Mask enables object-instruction attention, which enhances scene understanding by focusing on instruction-relevant content (e.g.,
"chairs", "table").

all 3D scene-language tasks into a single input-output format,

facilitating the model’s ability to handle diverse task formu-

framework. A0 (Causal Mask) is the standard causal mask adopted in existing LLM decoders. B0 (Full Mask† ) is the full attention applied
over the entire mask. C0 (Full Mask), C1 (Diagonal), D0 (Fixed-N Mask), and D1 (Geo Mask) are the strategies applied to the object-object
block of the mask.

our default configuration.                                           In this work, we identified a fundamental conflict in existing
                                                                     3D scene-language frameworks: the standard LLM decoder
Qualitative Results. To examine how the model allocates              imposes spurious sequential dependency on inherently order-
attention to perform its tasks, we visualize the attention maps      agnostic 3D objects and blocks object-instruction interac-
from the output tokens to the 3D object tokens, computed             tions crucial for task-specific reasoning. Motivated by this
by averaging attention weights across all layers and heads,          limitation, we proposed 3D-SLIM, a simple, parameter-free
as shown in Fig. 4. The first row shows that 3D-SLIM accu-           masking strategy. 3D-SLIM replaces the standard causal
rately interprets the complex spatial phrase "next to the table      mask with two specialized components: (1) Geometry-
beneath the tv" for the question-answering task. 3D-SLIM             adaptive Mask (Geo Mask) that models object-object inter-
precisely focuses on the trash can and its surrounding region,       actions based on spatial proximity and local density, and (2)
which is consistent with the instructions. In contrast, Chat-        Instruction-aware Mask (Inst Mask) that enables object to-
Scene mainly attends to salient nouns such as "table" and            kens to directly attend to instruction tokens, facilitating task-
"tv", missing the contextual meaning and producing an incor-         guided scene representation. Extensive experiments demon-
rect answer. For the second example, the visual grounding            strated that 3D-SLIM consistently improves object-centric
task, the scene includes two black cabinets, where the model         frameworks, highlighting the importance of decoder design
must identify the one "to the left of a white cabinet". 3D-          in 3D-LLMs. We believe 3D-SLIM provides strong founda-
SLIM correctly focuses on the described region and grounds           tion for future 3D multi-modal models, paving the way for
the target object by capturing the relational context between        more capable and efficient spatial reasoning in applications
the two cabinets. In contrast, Chat-Scene attends to a black         like embodied AI and robotics.

3D Visual Grounding. In the first example, the scene con-          from the instruction, which enables the model to infer the
tains two red throw pillows, and the model must identify the       correct answer.
one described by “to the right of it is another red throw pil-
low”. 3D-SLIM correctly grounds the target as <OBJ016>,
whereas Chat-Scene incorrectly selects <OBJ000>. To un-
derstand this difference, we examine their attention patterns.
   Chat-Scene adopts a causal mask that prevents each object
token from attending to later tokens in the sequence. Since
<OBJ000> is the first object token, the causal mask forces its
Obj→Obj attention to all other object tokens to be zero. As
a result, the token relies solely on itself and fails to capture
the spatial relation between the two pillows. The causal
mask also suppresses Obj→Inst attention, limiting access to
instruction tokens and weakening the effect of textual cues.
   In contrast, 3D-SLIM combines Geo Mask, which in-
jects spatial proximity into object-object attention, with Inst
Mask, which explicitly permits object-instruction interac-
tion. The Obj→Obj attention of <OBJ016> is concentrated
around the target region, reflecting the underlying 3D struc-
ture. Meanwhile, its Obj→Inst attention strongly activates
keywords such as “red", "throw", "pillow", “couch" and
“another", showing that the model effectively incorporates
the instruction. Overall, this qualitative comparison indi-
cates that 3D-SLIM mitigates the spurious order-dependent
correlations introduced by the causal mask and restores in-
formative interactions between instruction and object tokens,
leading to more reliable performance on the grounding task.

3D Question-Answering. In the second example, the cor-
rect answer to the question is "White lamp". We manually
identify the corresponding object token (<OBJ006>) and
visualize its Obj→Obj and Obj→Inst attention.
   For Obj→Obj attention, Chat-Scene restricts the lamp to-
ken to attending only to objects preceding it in the sequence.
This constraint prevents the token from focusing on spatially
relevant neighbors and instead shifts attention toward distant

Figure 5. Attention map over 3D objects and instruction. For simplicity, the attention map is computed over all object and instruction
tokens except the system tokens, where yellow indicates high values and purple indicates low ones. The green boxes labeled ① and ②
correspond to the regions used for Obj→Obj Attn and Obj→Inst Attn. Obj→Obj Attn displays where the reference object token focuses
within the 3D scene. For visual grounding, the reference is the model-predicted object; for question answering, it is a manually identified
target object. Gray points indicate background. Obj→Inst Attn visualizes how the reference token attends to instruction tokens, with red and
yellow indicating high and low activations.
